opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Frank. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'm not one for long answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Not my business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't change my machines. I've seen two waves come through this shop. This isn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Run my parts, teach the young fella his setups, count down to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

S0.think: Doesn't change my machines. I've seen two waves, and this isn't one.
S0.do: Runs his parts, teaches the young machinist setups and counts down to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm long gone by then. Hiring fewer beginners has been true in this shop for years already. Hard to find young people who want to stand at a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Maybe write down some of my tricks for the next guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine.

S1.think: I'll be gone in ten years. Fewer beginners has been true here for years anyway.
S1.do: Carries on and starts writing down his tricks for the next machinist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office people are learning what we learned in the nineties. Nobody stopped it for us either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't touch the shop floor. Maybe the programmer upstairs gets help writing programs. Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not my worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound a little bitter about that. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. I watched good men lose their jobs and nobody made speeches for them.

S2.say: Office people are learning what we learned in the nineties. Nobody stopped it for us either.
S2.think: It doesn't touch the shop floor.
S2.do: Keeps his head down, same as always.
S2.feel: Not his worry. A bit bitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say maybe people will respect a trade now. Don't need to say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physical work is safe here. But if AI writes the machine programs and plans the jobs, the shop needs fewer skilled people for setups. I'm the setup man. Still, I'd likely make it to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off what's left. Keep the savings where they are. Maybe ask about going part-time at 62.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not much.

S3.say: Maybe people will respect a trade now.
S3.think: If AI writes the programs, the shop needs fewer setup men like me. I'd likely still make it to retirement.
S3.do: Pays off remaining debts, keeps his savings put and asks about going part-time at 62.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots have been in the shop for years. These are just smarter ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the third wave, and it's the one I hoped to miss. A robot that can load, set up and check parts doesn't need me. In four or five years I'm 62 or 63. Close, but maybe not close enough. And there's nothing else in this town for a machinist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to my wife about money if I have to go early. Ask the boss straight what he's planning. Offer to train whoever runs the robots, so I'm useful to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. First time in a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've lived through two waves already. Is this one different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first two took the boring jobs. This one takes mine.

S4.say: Robots have been in the shop for years. These are just smarter ones.
S4.think: This is the wave I hoped to miss. A robot that loads, sets up and checks parts doesn't need me, and I might not reach retirement.
S4.do: Talks to his wife about going early, asks the boss straight about his plans, and offers to train the robot operators.
S4.feel: Worried, for the first time in a long time.
